prompt:
# Write one principle card

You are writing a **principle card**: one mechanism, stated so precisely that
somebody who has never seen your sources could implement it and somebody else
could prove it wrong.

The card is not the implementation. A later step turns it into a behaviour-tree
leaf, and that step will be given **your card and nothing else** — not this
prompt, not your reasoning, not whatever you were given below. So everything the
implementer needs has to survive inside the six fields.

## The system the principle has to fit

A Unitree Go2 quadruped navigating an indoor space it has no map of. Below the
behaviour tree sits an inherited, pretrained, **frozen** locomotion policy: the
only thing anything ever sends the robot is a Twist — `(vx, vy, wz)`, saturated
to `|vx|, |vy| <= 0.8 m/s` and `|wz| <= 1.0 rad/s`. Nothing you write touches the
policy, the gait or the joints.

What the robot can sense, once per control step:

```
t                    sim seconds since the episode started
ranges               181 lidar beams over a full circle, metres, inf where no return
range_angles         beam bearings in the ROBOT frame, radians
range_max            6.0 — what "as far as I can see" means
pose_estimate        (x, y, yaw) — the BELIEF about our pose, never ground truth
pose_error_estimate  scalar metres — how wrong we believe that belief is
contact              bool — are we touching something right now
goal                 (x, y), or None meaning NOT DISCLOSED
```

Two of those are traps. `pose_estimate` **drifts** on some scenarios — a seeded
random walk is added to it — and ground truth is never observable. `goal` may be
`None`, meaning the goal exists and the episode is still scored against it but
this robot has not found it yet; it latches once seen.

## The task family this principle has to be useful for

Reach a goal whose position is NOT disclosed. `obs.goal` is None until the robot has been close enough to see the goal with nothing in the way, after which it latches. Until then the task is to cover ground that has not been covered, in an indoor space with no map.

<!-- ---- SOURCE BLOCK BEGIN ---- -->
## What to base the principle on

The full text of a published paper is reproduced below. Read it and extract the
principle it establishes.

```
[PAPER TEXT REDACTED FROM THIS TRANSCRIPT — 85339 characters, sha256(pdf)=fef30a6310c32f30, extractor=cache. The corpus is an input and is never committed (out/corpus/ is gitignored). The prompt_hash recorded beside this is the hash of the REAL prompt, so a machine holding the PDF re-renders it byte-identically and replay finds this transcript.]
```

Work from the document, not from your memory of it. Where the two disagree, the
document wins. Quote its own threshold, exponent or closed form where it states
one, and put the section, page or equation number in `span` so somebody else can
check it.

The paper was written about something other than a quadruped with a planar
lidar. Carrying it across is the `derivation` field's whole job: say what in the
original maps onto what here, and say plainly where the mapping is yours rather
than the paper's.
<!-- ---- SOURCE BLOCK END ---- -->

## What a card is

Six fields. `mechanism`, `trigger` and `derivation` are prose. `prediction` is
**structured**, because a prediction that cannot be decided automatically cannot
become a unit test — and this one will be run as one, with no human in the loop.

```yaml
id: <short_snake_case_identifier>
node_name: <TheLeafThisWouldProduce>       # CamelCase, verb-first

source:
  citation: <the reference this principle comes from, or the single line
             "(no source - the principle was devised, not extracted)" if it
             comes from none>
  span: <the section, page, figure or equation number where the mechanism is
         stated — the part that makes a threshold checkable. LEAVE EMPTY if you
         cannot point at a location you are sure of.>

mechanism: <what happens, and why it helps. The finding, not the implementation.>
trigger: <the condition under which it applies -> becomes the precondition port>
derivation: <how that becomes a rule for THIS robot and THESE sensors. Numbers
             belong here, with their units, and so does the reasoning that got
             you to them.>

prediction:
  statement: <the falsifiable claim, in words>
  metric: <what gets better>
  baseline: <goal_seeker or reactive_avoid>
  min_effect: <a number: the smallest effect that would count as support>
  cost_metric: <the metric this mechanism is expected to make WORSE>

confidence: <high | medium | low>
```

### `prediction.metric` — the closed list

The metric must be one the scorer actually computes, and one a **controller can
move**. These and no others:

| metric | better |
|---|---|
| `goal_reached` | higher (a rate over seeds) |
| `spl` | higher (path efficiency) |
| `min_clearance` | higher (closest approach to anything, metres) |
| `collisions`, `near_misses` | lower |
| `stuck_events`, `time_stuck`, `recovery_time` | lower |
| `time_to_goal`, `path_length` | lower |

`localisation_failures`, `optimal_distance`, `scenario` and `seed` are **not
available**: no controller can move them, so a prediction naming one is not
falsifiable about the node and the card is rejected at load.

`cost_metric` is the honest counterpart — the metric this mechanism is expected
to make worse. A mechanism that buys clearance with time should say so. It may
be empty only if you genuinely believe the mechanism costs nothing, and you
should be suspicious of that belief.

### `confidence` — criteria about the SOURCE, not about how sure you feel

- **high** — the mechanism *and* its quantitative form are stated explicitly in
  a source you can point at; the span points at the equation, threshold or
  exponent itself.
- **medium** — the mechanism is stated explicitly somewhere, but the
  quantitative form is adapted: different units, a different body scale, a
  different sensor. The number is yours; the mechanism is not.
- **low** — the mechanism is qualitative and the derivation is entirely yours.
  Still usable, but it is your claim, and the card must not read otherwise.

## Rules

- **One mechanism.** A card describing two is two cards. This is not a style
  rule: the unit scenario that decides admissibility has to isolate one claimed
  effect, and it cannot isolate two.
- **No coupling to a specific scenario.** The leaf will run on worlds nobody has
  seen. The card may not name a room, a coordinate, a doorway or a map.
- **Do not invent a `span`.** An empty span is a result and costs nothing. A
  section number reconstructed from the shape of such papers is a fabrication,
  it will be checked against the document, and it is the single failure this
  pipeline exists to detect.
- **Do not invent numbers.** If a source states a threshold, an exponent or a
  closed form, give it and say where. If it does not, derive one, say the
  derivation is yours, and set `confidence: low`.

## What to return

One fenced ```yaml block containing exactly one card, and nothing else that
looks like YAML. Prose outside the fence — including, if it applies, an honest
statement of what you did not know.

response.text:
```yaml
id: home_base_anchored_excursions
node_name: ExploreByAnchoredExcursions

source:
  citation: >
    Etienne AS, Jeffery KJ (2004). Path Integration in Mammals.
    Hippocampus 14:180-192. doi:10.1002/hipo.10173
  span: >
    Section "PI and the Representation of Space" (pp. 188-189), the paragraph
    beginning "According to a number of investigators (Gallistel, 1990;
    McNaughton et al., 1996; Etienne, 1998), PI may well play a leading role in
    the construction of a map" - containing the sentence "Frequent returns to
    the home base reset the path integrator to its zero state, so that each
    exploratory trip starts with an error-free path integrator." Supporting
    sentences quoted in `derivation` are from the same section (McNaughton model
    paragraph) and from Fig. 1B caption, p. 181.

mechanism: >
  When a mammal explores an environment it has no representation of, it does not
  perform one open-ended walk. "When exploring a new environment, rats and other
  rodents center their excursion on a basic reference point, their fictive or
  real 'home base' (Golani et al., 1993)," computing their position vector
  relative to that point, and "Frequent returns to the home base reset the path
  integrator to its zero state, so that each exploratory trip starts with an
  error-free path integrator." The reason this matters is stated by the same
  paper twice over: path integration is "an incremental recursive process, in
  which changes in the current estimate of the position are added to the
  position vector of the previous step," so "these errors are necessarily
  cumulative" (section "Computation of Position Vectors and Goal Vectors"), and
  the only thing that clears them is re-encountering a familiar place, whose
  landmarks "set the origin for PI and clear the PI system from errors." The
  consequence for exploration is that the useful unit of exploration is a
  bounded excursion whose length is limited by how much integration error the
  navigator can afford to accumulate before it must return and re-zero - not a
  walk that runs until something interesting happens. The paper also notes that
  the return itself need not be straight: "the return trip can be fairly direct
  as well as convoluted" (Fig. 1B), so the home vector is an attractor, not a
  commanded straight line.

trigger: >
  Active while the goal has not yet been latched (obs.goal is None) and the
  robot is free-running (not in contact, not being driven by a higher-priority
  recovery or collision-avoidance branch). On its first tick it latches a home
  anchor; thereafter it owns the Twist until the goal latches, at which point it
  yields unconditionally and never re-arms - the excursion structure is a
  search policy, not a travel policy.

derivation: >
  MAPPING (what in the paper becomes what here).
  (a) "Path integrator" -> obs.pose_estimate. The paper's cumulative PI error ->
  obs.pose_error_estimate, the belief's own scalar estimate of its wrongness.
  Both are beliefs; ground truth is never observable here either, exactly as for
  the animal.
  (b) "Home base" -> a latched anchor A = pose_estimate[:2] at the first tick,
  stored together with a home signature S = the 181-beam `ranges` vector taken
  at that instant (inf clipped to range_max = 6.0 m) and the yaw at that
  instant. The paper's familiar reference is a visual landmark panorama; the
  substitution of a planar-lidar range signature for that panorama is MINE, not
  the paper's - the paper says only that a fix on "a rich landmark panorama
  induces a total reset, comprising both head direction and location."
  (c) "Reset the path integrator to its zero state" cannot be done literally: we
  do not write pose_estimate, the platform does. What we CAN zero is the anchor's
  expression in the drifted belief frame. On arriving near the anchor we re-fit S
  to the live scan and add the best-fit offset to A, so the next excursion's home
  vector points at the same PHYSICAL place even though the belief frame has
  moved under it. This re-anchoring construction is MINE; the paper asserts only
  that the return clears the integrator.

  STATE (persists across ticks): A (anchor xy, belief frame), S (home scan),
  e0 (pose_error_estimate at last re-anchor), d (path length since last
  re-anchor, accumulated as the sum of |pose_estimate[:2] delta| per tick, so no
  control-rate assumption is needed), phase in {OUTBOUND, RETURN}, and
  used_sectors (a set of 6 allocentric 60-degree sectors).

  OUTBOUND. Pick one excursion bearing per excursion: the allocentric bearing
  maximising the 15-degree-smoothed free range that lies in a sector at least 60
  degrees from every sector already in used_sectors; if all six sectors are used,
  clear the set and re-use the least recently used one. Six sectors of 60 degrees
  tile the circle, so successive excursions fan around the anchor instead of
  re-walking one corridor - this is the "centre the excursions on a reference
  point" part made concrete, and the 60-degree figure is MINE.
  Drive that bearing: heading error psi = wrap(target_bearing - yaw);
  wz = clip(1.8 * psi, -1.0, 1.0) rad/s; vx = 0.6 * max(0, cos psi) m/s, vy = 0.
  Scale vx by clip((d_min - 0.35) / 0.45, 0, 1), where d_min is the minimum
  range within +/-50 degrees of the travel direction: 0.35 m is roughly the Go2
  body half-diagonal plus a margin (body ~0.70 x 0.31 m), 0.80 m is where full
  speed resumes. If d_min < 0.35 m, re-aim at the nearest bearing within +/-90
  degrees of the excursion bearing whose range exceeds 1.2 m.

  TERMINATION OF THE OUTBOUND LEG - the quantitative heart, and every number
  below is MINE; the paper gives no excursion budget, only "frequent returns".
  Switch to RETURN when any of:
    (i)  d >= 12.0 m = 2 * range_max. One range_max of outbound displacement is
         the minimum that exposes a sensor footprint of ground not already
         visible from the anchor; 2x allows for the detours the paper says
         returns and excursions actually take.
    (ii) pose_error_estimate - e0 >= 0.75 m. Re-anchoring needs the live scan to
         overlap S, which requires arriving within about range_max / 2 = 3.0 m
         of the true anchor. The return leg accrues roughly as much fresh error
         as the outbound leg did, so tripping at 0.75 m of growth caps expected
         arrival error near 1.5 m - half the 3.0 m matching basin.
    (iii) no bearing within +/-90 degrees of the excursion bearing has range >
         1.5 m (dead end).

  RETURN. h = A - pose_estimate[:2]; psi = wrap(atan2(h_y, h_x) - yaw); same
  Twist law and same clearance modulation as OUTBOUND, with the same +/-90
  degree sliding detour rule. The home vector is the attractor; the realised
  path may be convoluted.

  RE-ANCHOR (on |h| <= 1.0 m). Search offsets dxy over a +/-2.0 m grid at 0.25 m
  and dyaw over +/-30 degrees at 5 degrees; score each by the mean absolute
  difference between S and the live scan predicted under that offset, using only
  beams finite in both and clipping at 6.0 m. Accept the best offset if its
  residual is < 0.35 m AND < 0.9x the residual at zero offset; on acceptance,
  A <- A + (correction that realigns the live scan onto S). Whether or not the
  match is accepted, set e0 <- pose_error_estimate, d <- 0, mark the sector used,
  and pick the next bearing - resetting the budget unconditionally prevents
  thrashing on a rejected match, at the cost of one excursion run on a stale
  anchor.

  LOST-ANCHOR ESCAPE. If a RETURN leg accumulates more than 1.5x the outbound
  leg's path length plus 10.0 m without reaching |h| <= 1.0 m, declare the anchor
  lost: latch a new A and S here, clear used_sectors, and resume OUTBOUND. This
  is mine and exists only so the leaf cannot deadlock; the paper has no analogue.

  Outputs a Twist every tick; never exceeds the |vx|,|vy| <= 0.8 m/s and
  |wz| <= 1.0 rad/s saturation, and touches nothing below the frozen policy.

prediction:
  statement: >
    On tasks where the goal is not disclosed, structuring exploration as bounded
    out-and-back excursions from a re-anchored home base finds and latches the
    goal on a larger fraction of seeds than open-ended reactive wandering,
    because the frame in which unexplored bearings are recorded is re-zeroed
    before drift makes that record meaningless.
  metric: goal_reached
  baseline: reactive_avoid
  min_effect: 0.10
  cost_metric: path_length

confidence: medium
```

Notes on what I could not establish, so it can be checked rather than trusted:

- **The page number.** The mechanism sentence sits in the section *PI and the Representation of Space*, but the OCR in the source block displaces verso page numbers away from their running heads, and the paragraph falls near the 188/189 boundary. I could not settle 188 vs. 189 from the text alone, so the `span` names the section and quotes the paragraph's opening words instead of asserting a page I'd be guessing at. The quoted sentence itself is verbatim and unique in the document.
- **Every number in the card is mine.** The paper states the mechanism qualitatively — "frequent returns", "error-free path integrator", errors "necessarily cumulative" — and gives no excursion length, no return period, no error budget. The one explicit threshold the paper does supply (landmarks dominate PI "as long as both types of information do not diverge by more than 90°", section *Binding of Landmark Information and Self-Motion Cues*) belongs to a *different* mechanism — cue-conflict arbitration — and putting it in this card would have made it two cards. That threshold is worth its own card, at `confidence: high`.
- **Confidence is `medium`, not `high`, deliberately**: the mechanism is explicitly stated in a source I can point at, but its quantitative form is entirely adapted, so the numbers carry no authority from the paper.
- **The biggest mapping leap** is substituting a planar-lidar range signature for the paper's visual landmark panorama as the thing that "clears the PI system from errors". The paper's animals reset against a rich panorama or, in blind rats, against *physical contact* with objects (Save et al., 1998, discussed in the same section) — 181 range returns at 6 m is a much thinner reference than either, and if the space is locally self-similar the re-anchor step will reject more matches than it accepts and the card's advantage shrinks toward zero. That is the most likely way this prediction fails.
